newsitem.title: UK: New York's NYMEX exchange plots global advance.
newsitem.headline: New York's NYMEX exchange plots global advance.

text.p: The New York Mercantile Exchange, already the biggest physical commodity exchange in the world, is tapping its renewed confidence to launch a string of products on several continents as it senses the regulatory tide turning in its favour back home.

NYMEX's after-hours ACCESS electronic trading system has become the tool for prising open foreign markets for the exchange's U.S. deliverable contracts, tilling the ground so that new, locally deliverable contracts take root later.
"NYMEX ACCESS gave us a lot of confidence - it's the most successful proprietary electronic trading system in the world," the exchange's chairman, Daniel Rappaport told reporters in London.
NYMEX's contracts are already traded on ACCESS terminals in Sydney and London, and will be available in Hong Kong from the first quarter of next year to crude oil, gold, silver and copper trading.

"What we would like to do is to work with the Hong Kong Futures Exchange to develop Asian-based energy and metals contracts," Rappaport said. "Latin America and Asia are the biggest growth potential for metals and energy."

The exchange is also in advanced talks with the Singapore International Monetary Exchange to introduce ACCESS trading in the island state. And wood pulp and ethanol trading in Brazil's Sao Paulo may also be on the cards later on.
ACCESS trading volumes were up 20 percent this year to 5,000 contracts a day, Rappaport said.

Some of the exchange's new found confidence also flows from NYMEX's success in helping to convince Congress the U.S. Commodity Exchange Act, passed in 1972, needed updating to give regulatory watchdog Commodity Futures Trading Commission, powers over foreign exchanges in the U.S.
The London Metal Exchange trades the world's dominant copper futures contract, and it opened copper warehouses in the U.S. in April 1995, prompting some to predict the demise of COMEX's contract.
"It seems like the rumours of the death of the COMEX contract were greatly exaggerated," Rappaport said.
NYMEX is taking a leaf from the LME's own book and looking hard at opening copper warehouses in Singapore and Chile.

Rappaport said the number of contracts traded in copper in New York rose since the Sumitomo scandal rocked the LME in June - an event which NYMEX quickly seized to underscore what it considers to be regulatory deficiencies on LME.
"We do feel compelled to use Sumitomo as an opportunity to highlight all the things we have been saying in the previous two years," Rappaport said.
He added the message also hit home in London. "The LME used to ignore and now they insult us."

Meanwhile NYMEX is likely to ask the CFTC next year for permission to trade futures contracts for coal and, if regulatory changes are made in the U.S., a new aluminium futures contract will be launched to compete on a second front with the LME.
Also next year NYMEX celebrates its 125th anniversary by moving into a brand new $225 million trading floor in New York's Battery Park City overlooking the Hudson River.
